title: Engines and humans 3: using an engine to learn
outcomes: Writes a one-sentence verdict (move, threat, plan) for a position before asking an engine, then compares ideas before numbers
Reads an engine score with its sign, its depth and a mate score, and says in plain words who is better and by roughly how much
Reads an engine line by saying what each move threatens and what it stops, and says why the first move is advice and the rest evidence
Shows with two boards why the engine's best move is not always the best teaching move
Names one pattern behind three blunders (the capturing piece was a guard) and asks what a piece was doing before it captures or trades
Uses the app's Analysis page (lines, depth, whole-game analysis, next mistake, learn from your mistakes, show threats) inside a small review routine

steps.text: **Two moves, two ideas.** At depth 16 the engine put Re1 first, with h3, b4 and Nbd2 each within a tenth of a pawn [V, one run]. A gap that small is invisible in play. The difference you can feel is the idea: one plan restrains Black and gains queenside space, the other finishes development first. [I] Both are ordinary here: the number cannot choose, your reason can.

steps.prompt: Which plan did you prefer, and can you give a reason that does not use a number? If your reason was a move name, rewrite it as an idea.

steps.text: **The question and the method.** Can you review a game engine-last, find the pattern behind a blunder, and read a score and a line the way a teacher would? Engine-last means: one, look and name a threat, a weak spot and a plan; two, write one sentence of why; three, only then ask the engine; four, compare ideas before numbers. That order is our own design decision, not a tested result.

steps.text: **Reading a score.** The number is pawns from White's side: plus one (100 centipawns) means White is about a pawn ahead, minus one means Black is. 'M3' means mate in three. 'Depth 16' means the main lines reached about sixteen half-moves; some go deeper, some shallower [R]. [I] Rough words: under half a pawn level, up to one and a half a small edge, up to three a clear edge, beyond that decisive.

**What a pawn is worth to a person.** The score assumes both sides play perfectly from here. *Win chance* turns it into odds: in the app's formula plus one pawn is about 59 per cent for White and plus three about 75 [V, arithmetic checked]. [I] For club players the practical chances are probably closer to level, since nobody plays perfectly. The marks ?!, ? and ?? later measure lost win chance.

steps.text: **One pattern, from real games.** The Lichess puzzle file we hold has 6,157,341 puzzles; 224,023 carry the tag *hangingPiece*. In 125,348 of those the first move, the mistake that creates the puzzle, is a capture. In 26,506 (about 12 per cent of all hangingPiece puzzles) the reply takes a different piece the capturing piece had been guarding [V, our count]. Puzzles are chosen because a tactic exists: a catalogue of mistakes, not a frequency in play.

steps.text: **One question for all three.** Before a capture, a trade or a 'free pawn', ask: *what was this piece doing before it moved?* If the answer is 'guarding something', keep guarding, or make sure the guarded piece is safe another way. [I] The habit works because attention follows the prize; the question moves attention to what you give up.

**The Analysis page, step by step** [V, read in the app source on 30 Oct 2026]. Load a game as text, or set up a position. Choose how many lines and what depth. *Analyse whole game* scores every position at depth 12 and marks moves: ?! loses 10 to 20 points of win chance, ? 20 to 30, ?? 30 or more. *Next mistake* and *Learn from your mistakes* visit the ? and ?? moves only.

steps.prompt: Guided exercise, no screenshots needed. Open Analysis with a game you lost. Before you press anything, write your own list: the three moments you felt unsure. Then run the whole-game analysis and count how many of your three the tool also marked.

steps.text: **Two more buttons.** *Learn from your mistakes* returns to the position before an error and asks you for a better move; press *Show the answer* only after you have written your own sentence. *Show threats* draws one red arrow: the first move the engine would play if it were the opponent's turn. The next board shows what it would draw for Black at move 17.

steps.caption: What Show threats would draw here: one arrow, the white queen's move to h7. The bishop on d3 that backs it is not drawn: you must see that yourself. Use the button after you have written your own threat, not before.

steps.text: **What others say.** As summarised on pages we could read, Jeremy Silman puts a tactical check first and treats engine output as the what, not the why [S]. Jacob Aagaard argues that serious errors often start at the very beginning of a calculation, when a candidate move is never considered [S, a reviewer's account]. Mark Dvoretsky's school stressed analysing your own games [R, from memory]. None of this tests engine-last review; they are directions to try.

fields.label: the question that would have caught it:

steps.text: **Three habits that waste an engine.** One, shown above: playing its line without knowing why. Two: trusting a small plus in a quiet position; a score near plus one half is within what both sides can reach with sensible play [I]. Three: analysing only your losses. [H] Wins hide errors too. [H] Reading the engine's answer before trying may feel like learning without being so; this is our conjecture.

steps.prompt: Which of the three habits is yours? Write one sentence about the last time you did it.

fields.label: my habit, and the last time:

steps.text: **Where engines mislead.** Three cases. Depth: the same position gave -1.3 at depth 2 and a forced mate at depth 6 [V, earlier board]. Perfect play: the score assumes both sides play exactly, so a plus that needs ten precise moves may be worth little to you [I]. Fortresses: when the side ahead cannot make progress against best defence, a large number can hide a draw [R, endgame books; we did not check a position here].

**Compare ideas with several lines.** The Lines setting in Analysis shows more than one engine choice. Set it to 3 on the Ruy Lopez position from earlier and hide the scores in your mind. For each of the three first moves, write what it is for in one sentence. Then compare the ideas. [H] Choosing between ideas for your own reasons trains judgement more than reading which number is largest.

steps.prompt: Open the Ruy Lopez position in Analysis with Lines set to 3. Write the idea of each first move before you look at its score, then say which idea you prefer and why.

steps.text: **A weekly routine [H].** After a game that mattered: replay it without the engine and mark the moments you felt unsure (ten minutes). Run whole-game analysis and open only the three biggest swings, writing your sentence before each answer (ten minutes). Name the pattern in one word and add it to a list (two minutes). Once a week, pick one pattern to watch for. Cut any step you will not do.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. A club teammate says: 'I just look at what the engine says after my game.' Explain engine-last review to them in your own words.

steps.text: **Teach-back checklist.** Did you (1) ask your listener for a sentence before showing the engine, (2) name the pattern, (3) give one example they could set up on a board, (4) give one warning? A missing item is the one to practise.

**Recap.** Write before you ask; compare ideas, then numbers. The first move is advice, the rest is evidence. Before a capture ask what the piece was guarding. [H] Keep one habit: a sentence of why before the engine. **Check yourself:** minus means Black is better; depth is how far the search looked; for a line, say what each move threatens and stops; drop the habit you named.

steps.prompt: Your engine habits. Write one habit you will start, one you will stop, and the first game you will use them on.
